extracted.intended_audience: federal agency rulemaking officials, records custodians, counsel, and policymakers
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for federal agencies on compiling, preserving, indexing, certifying, and disclosing rulemaking records for notice-and-comment rulemaking, and on whether, when, and how to use social media in rulemaking and related outreach.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition: Rulemaking record
rubrics_metrics.description: "Rulemaking record" means the full record of materials before the agency in an informal rulemaking.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Conference contemplates that, in addition to materials required by law to be included in the rulemaking record, as well as all comments and materials submitted to the agency during comment periods, any material that the agency considered should be included as part of that record.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition: "Considered" (inclusion standard)
rubrics_metrics.description: "Considered" entails review by an individual with substantive responsibilities in connection with the rulemaking and some minimum degree of attention to the contents of a document.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A document should generally be included if an individual with substantive responsibilities reviewed it to evaluate its possible significance for the rulemaking, unless the review disclosed it was not germane. Documents should not be excluded because the reviewer disagreed with their analysis or because the agency did not or will not rely on them. The concept is interpreted to generate a body of materials by which the rule can be evaluated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition: Public rulemaking docket
rubrics_metrics.description: "Public rulemaking docket" means the public version of the rulemaking record managed by the agency, regardless of location, such as online at Regulations.gov or an agency website or available for physical review in a docket room.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The public docket includes all information the agency has made available for public viewing. Agencies should manage public dockets to achieve maximum disclosure, though prudential concerns (e.g., copyrighted or indecent materials) may limit online display. Best practice: describe and note online materials not displayed but available for physical inspection. Include materials generated and considered after the close of comment period but prior to issuance of the final rule when appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition: Administrative record for judicial review
rubrics_metrics.description: "Administrative record for judicial review" means the materials tendered by the agency and certified to a court as the record on review of the agency’s regulatory action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The administrative record provided to the court should include an affidavit by a certifying official attesting to contents and accuracy and should include an index itemizing contents. Parties often rely on the index to designate portions for judicial review (e.g., joint appendix).

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of protected or privileged materials
rubrics_metrics.description: Some materials in the rulemaking record may be protected from public disclosure by law or withheld on basis of privilege (e.g., classified information, confidential business information, trade secrets, attorney-client privilege, attorney work product, pre-decisional deliberative process privilege).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agency practices vary. The Conference recommends agencies develop a written policy for treatment of protected or privileged materials, including indexing, in public rulemaking dockets and in certification of the administrative record for judicial review, and make that policy publicly available.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presumption of regularity in compilation and agency control
rubrics_metrics.description: Compilation and preparation of the administrative record for judicial review is properly within the province of the agency and should be accorded a presumption of regularity by the reviewing court.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Completion or supplementation of the record may be appropriate only where a strong showing overcomes the presumption (e.g., strong showing of bad faith or improper behavior). Courts may inquire into allegations that the agency omitted information that should have been included.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rulemaking record — required contents (recommended)
rubrics_metrics.description: In the absence of a specific statutory requirement to the contrary, the agency rulemaking record in an informal rulemaking proceeding should include listed categories of materials.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specifically recommended inclusions: (a) notices pertaining to the rulemaking; (b) comments and other materials submitted to the agency related to the rulemaking; (c) transcripts or recordings, if any, of oral presentations made in the course of a rulemaking; (d) reports or recommendations of any relevant advisory committees; (e) other materials required by statute, executive order, or agency rule to be considered or to be made public in connection with the rulemaking; and (f) any other materials considered by the agency during the course of the rulemaking.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public rulemaking docket — scope of disclosure
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies should manage public rulemaking dockets to achieve maximum public disclosure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To the extent feasible, public dockets should include all materials in the rulemaking record, subject to legal limitations on disclosure, claims of privilege, or statutory exclusions the agency invokes. It may be prudent not to include certain sensitive information online and instead note its availability for physical review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Administrative record for judicial review — contents exclusions
rubrics_metrics.description: The administrative record provided to the court should contain all materials in the rulemaking record except materials protected from disclosure by law or those the agency properly withholds under legal standards (including privilege).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agencies need not include privileged or legally protected materials in the record submitted to courts, but they should document and index contents and provide affidavits attesting to accuracy when certifying the record.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timing of compilation
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies should begin compiling rulemaking records no later than the date on which an agency publishes the notice of proposed rulemaking.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agencies should include materials considered in preparation of the NPRM (e.g., responses to advance notices or notices of inquiry) and continue compiling the rulemaking record as long as the rule is pending before the agency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Designation of custodians
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies should designate one or more custodians for rulemaking recordkeeping, either on a rulemaking-by-rulemaking basis or generally.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agencies should inform personnel of custodian(s) and direct deposit of rulemaking record materials with them (except necessary confidential information with restricted access). Custodians should document the record compilation process.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indexing public rulemaking dockets
rubrics_metrics.description: To the extent practicable, agencies should index public rulemaking dockets for informal rulemaking at an appropriate level of detail.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Indexing aids public understanding and supports designation of portions of the administrative record for judicial review; indexes are often used by parties in preparing joint appendices.

rubrics_metrics.name: NARA guidance on rulemaking records
rubrics_metrics.description: The National Archives and Records Administration (NARA) should amend its agency guidance to address the official status and legal value of records relating to informal rulemaking, particularly administrative records for judicial review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This addresses the need for clarity on the archival and legal treatment of electronic and informal rulemaking records.

rubrics_metrics.name: Electronic records management and transfer to NARA
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies using electronic records management systems to manage rulemaking records should work with NARA to ensure adequacy for recordkeeping and transfer of permanent records.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agencies should review records schedules given developments in electronic records management and ensure systems (e.g., Federal Document Management System or agency-specific systems) support preservation and legal requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Certification procedures for administrative records
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies should develop procedures for designating appropriate individuals to certify administrative records to the court in case of judicial review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agency certifications should include an index of contents of the administrative record for judicial review. Certifying individuals may or may not be record custodians.

rubrics_metrics.name: Agency policy and public availability on protected/privileged materials
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies should develop a general policy regarding treatment of protected or privileged materials, including indexing, in public rulemaking dockets and in certification of the administrative record for judicial review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agencies should make this policy available to the public and provide it to the Department of Justice if DOJ represents the agency in litigation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Agency guidance for implementing best practices
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies that engage in informal rulemaking should issue guidance to aid personnel in implementing best practices for recordkeeping, and make their guidance publicly available and available to DOJ when applicable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance contents should vary with agency size and resources but should at minimum address: (a) essential components of the rulemaking record, public docket, and administrative record for judicial review; (b) appropriate exclusions (e.g., personal notes, drafts); (c) timing of compilation and indexing practices; (d) management/segregation of privileged materials (attorney work product, deliberative materials); (e) management/segregation of sensitive/protected materials (copyrighted, classified, protected personal, confidential supervisory/business information); (f) policies/procedures for protection of sensitive info submitted by the public; (g) preservation of records and dockets; (h) certification processes and identifying certifying official; and (i) capabilities and limitations of recordkeeping tools/technologies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judicial review — presumption of regularity
rubrics_metrics.description: A reviewing court should afford the administrative record for judicial review a presumption of regularity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This presumption supports agency designation of the administrative record absent clear evidence to the contrary; courts have permitted supplementation only upon strong showings (e.g., bad faith).

rubrics_metrics.name: Judicial review — supplementation/completion of the record
rubrics_metrics.description: In appropriate circumstances, a reviewing court should permit or require supplementation or completion of the record on review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Supplementation may be appropriate when the presumption of regularity is rebutted (strong showing of improper agency behavior or credible allegations that the record is incomplete). Courts have allowed limited discovery where strong showing of bad faith exists.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explore social media for rulemaking engagement
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies should explore in the rulemaking process the use of social media—online platforms that can provide broad opportunities for public consultation, discussion, and engagement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Social media include tools facilitating two-way communication, collaboration, interaction, or sharing (e.g., Facebook, Twitter, Ideascale, blogs, crowdsourcing platforms). Technology evolves quickly; guidance is intended to be tool-agnostic and encourage experimentation where appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use social media for public outreach and education
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies should use social media to inform and educate the public about agency activities, the rulemaking process generally, and specific rulemakings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agencies should post to agency websites and send notifications through multiple social channels to raise awareness, particularly among underrepresented stakeholders. Social media may be effective for reaching diffused affected interests.

rubrics_metrics.name: Outreach strategies to engage missing stakeholders (when using social media)
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies should recognize that raising awareness among missing stakeholders requires new outreach strategies beyond Federal Register, Regulations.gov, and agency website notices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider: (a) developing one or more evenhanded communications plans tailored to the rule and targeted stakeholders; (b) clearly explaining how the public can participate, the role of comments, and how comments will be used; (c) encouraging public response by explaining how the proposed rule affects participants and what input is most useful; (d) asking organizations to disseminate participation messages and encourage substantive individualized comments; and (e) using multilingual social media outlets where appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Agency-led education and exemplary comment resources
rubrics_metrics.description: The GSA, e-Rulemaking Program Management Office, and other agencies should create and distribute educational programs about rulemaking using social media.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Efforts could include producing videos about the rulemaking process and how to comment effectively, hosting webinars where agency personnel discuss drafting useful comments, maintaining an online database of exemplary comments, or offering classes/webinars in which officials review draft comments and suggest improvements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Automated updates on significant rulemakings
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies should explore ways to publicize and allow the public to receive regular, automated updates on developments in significant rulemakings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Automated notifications via social media channels can improve public awareness and ongoing engagement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use social media pre-NPRM for dispersed knowledge collection
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies should consider using social media prior to publication of an NPRM or proposed policy to understand current state of affairs, collect dispersed knowledge, or identify problems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To enhance value of public input, agencies should make clear the sort of information sought and how it will be used, acknowledge submissions, ask follow-up questions, and provide substantive responses to directly engage participants.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use social media for retrospective review and negotiated rulemaking support
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies should consider using social media in support of retrospective review of existing regulations and where collaborative input is useful (e.g., negotiated rulemaking).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Social media can help learn about actual experience under regulations and facilitate collaboration among diverse interests during and between meetings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate appropriateness and design before using social media in notice-and-comment
rubrics_metrics.description: Before using social media in connection with a particular rulemaking, agencies should identify specific goals and carefully consider potential costs and benefits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Social media may not be appropriate in all rulemakings. Success requires thoughtful identification of purposes, selection of appropriate tools, integration into the traditional comment process, and clear communication to the public about how discussions will be used. Agencies must consider legal requirements (APA, Paperwork Reduction Act, First Amendment, ex parte policies) and practical concerns (verification/identity of participants, effects of ranking/voting tools, need for facilitation).

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical and legal concerns about social media use
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies face legal uncertainties and practical doubts about whether, when, and how social media will benefit rulemaking.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Issues include whether public contributions via blogs/Facebook are "comments" under the APA (triggering obligations to review/respond and include in the rulemaking record), how the Paperwork Reduction Act applies, First Amendment limits on moderation, and applicability of ex parte communications policies. Practical concerns include low quality/participation, need for third-party facilitators to improve substantive input, whether to require participant identification, and risks that ranking/voting tools may mislead or be manipulated.
